1.title: Streaming Ingestion
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Streaming Ingestion. This module covers the task statement: perform data ingestion. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Read data from streaming sources: Amazon Kinesis, Amazon M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka), DynamoDB Streams, A W S D M S (Database Migration Service), A W S Glue and Amazon Redshift. Choose between Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose and Amazon M S K. Call a Lambda function from Kinesis and tune batches, errors and parallelism. Manage fan-in and fan-out of streaming data. Describe replayability of an ingestion pipeline. Tell stateful from stateless processing.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Tracks Its Trucks
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Tracks Its Trucks. two thousand trucks send a position and temperature reading every few seconds. Dispatchers need the map to update within seconds. The analytics team wants every reading in S three, in a query-friendly format. If a processing bug is found, they must be able to replay the last two days. Your job: choose the streaming services and set them up.

1.title: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits
1.text: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits. The figure shows this: Choosing a streaming source: Kinesis Data Streams for custom, replayable streams, Amazon Data Firehose for delivery to a store, Amazon M S K for Kafka, DynamoDB Streams for table changes, and A W S D M S for database changes.

1.title: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued
1.text: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. What it is: A managed, durable, ordered stream split into shards; you write the consumers. Pick it when: You need custom processing, several consumers, replay and second-level latency. Amazon Data Firehose. What it is: A managed delivery service with buffering, optional transformation and format conversion. Pick it when: You only need to load streaming data into S three, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables or an H T T P endpoint with no code. Amazon M S K. What it is: Managed Apache Kafka: brokers, topics, partitions, consumer groups. Pick it when: You already use Kafka or need the Kafka protocol and ecosystem.

1.title: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued
1.text: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued. DynamoDB Streams. What it is: An ordered log of item changes in one table, kept twenty-four hours. Pick it when: You must react to changes in a DynamoDB table. A W S D M S (C D C). What it is: Reads a database's change log and writes the changes to a target (S three, Kinesis, Kafka and more). Pick it when: You must stream database changes without touching the application. Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink. What it is: Managed Apache Flink for stateful stream processing. Pick it when: Windows, joins and aggregations over a stream. A W S Glue streaming jobs. What it is: Spark Structured Streaming E T L (extract, transform, load) that reads Kinesis or Kafka. Pick it when: Serverless stream E T L into S three or other stores.

1.title: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued
1.text: Streaming Sources and the Service That Fits, continued. Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion. What it is: A materialized view reads straight from Kinesis or M S K. Pick it when: Low-latency analytics in the warehouse with no staging in S three. Exam tip: Kinesis Data Streams equals you build and read the stream; Data Firehose equals it delivers for you. If the question says replay, multiple consumers or custom logic, it is Data Streams (or M S K). If it says load into S three or Redshift with no administration, it is Firehose.

1.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
1.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The figure shows this: Kinesis Data Streams: producers send records with a partition key, the key picks the shard, records stay in order inside a shard, and consumers read from each shard.

1.title: How it works
1.text: How it works. A stream has one or more shards; a record carries a partition key, a data blob and a sequence number. The partition key is hashed to choose the shard: the same key goes to the same shard, so order is kept per key (not across the whole stream). Producers: PutRecord or PutRecords (up to five hundred records per call), the Kinesis Producer Library (K P L) (batches and aggregates), the Kinesis Agent (files and logs), A W S S D K s (software development kit), IoT and other A W S services.

1.title: How it works, continued
1.text: How it works, continued. Consumers: the Kinesis Client Library (K C L) (tracks progress with checkpoints), A W S Lambda, Amazon Data Firehose, Managed Service for Apache Flink, A W S Glue, your own code.

1.title: Capacity modes and limits
1.text: Capacity modes and limits. On-demand. You manage: Nothing: shards scale automatically. Throughput: New streams start at four megabytes per second write and eight megabytes per second read and scale up (up to ten gigabytes per second write in the largest Regions). Provisioned. You manage: The number of shards (change with UpdateShardCount, split and merge). Throughput: Each shard: one megabytes per second or one thousand records per second write; two megabytes per second read. Record size: up to ten mebibytes before base sixty-four encoding (older material says one megabyte), designed for occasional large records. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Capacity modes and limits, continued
1.text: Capacity modes and limits, continued. Retention: twenty-four hours by default, configurable from twenty-four hours up to three hundred sixty-five days. Reading: each shard allows five GetRecords calls per second and two megabytes per second shared by all standard consumers. Throttling: writing above the shard limit raises ProvisionedThroughputExceededException; fix with more shards, a better partition key, batching and backoff. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Hot shards
1.text: Hot shards. A hot shard gets more traffic than its limit because many records share one partition key (for example one very busy truck or a constant key). Fix: use a key with many distinct values (truck I D plus a small random suffix), split the hot shard, or use on-demand mode. Exam tip: "Records for the same device must stay in order" to use the device I D as the partition key. "One shard is throttled while others are idle" to a hot partition key.

1.title: Amazon Data Firehose
1.text: Amazon Data Firehose. A fully managed delivery service: no shards to manage, it scales automatically. Sources: direct put from producers, a Kinesis data stream, M S K, CloudWatch Logs and events, IoT and more. Destinations: Amazon S three, Amazon Redshift (loads through S three with a copy command), Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables, H T T P endpoints and partner services. Near real time: it buffers by size and time and delivers when either is reached first (S three default: five mebibytes or three hundred seconds; the interval can be set from zero to nine hundred seconds; zero buffering trades more small objects for lower latency).

1.title: Amazon Data Firehose, continued
1.text: Amazon Data Firehose, continued. Optional features: a Lambda transformation, format conversion to Parquet or O R C (Optimized Row Columnar) (uses a schema from the Glue Data Catalog), dynamic partitioning (S three prefixes by record fields), source-record backup to another S three bucket. A record can be as large as one thousand kilobytes. Not a store: Firehose cannot replay; keep a Kinesis stream or an S three backup if you need replay. Exam tip: "Deliver streaming logs to S three as Parquet, partitioned by date, with no servers" to Data Firehose with format conversion and dynamic partitioning.

1.title: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)
1.text: Amazon M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka). Fully managed Apache Kafka: A W S runs the brokers (at least one per Availability Zone) and the controllers, and replaces failed brokers; existing Kafka clients and tools work unchanged. Concepts: topics are split into partitions; producers write, consumer groups read; each partition is read by one consumer per group. Cluster types: M S K Provisioned (Standard or Express brokers: you choose broker count and size) and M S K Serverless (no capacity to manage). M S K Connect runs Kafka Connect connectors to stream data to and from other systems; M S K Replicator copies data between clusters.

1.title: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka), continued
1.text: Amazon M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka), continued. Retention is set per topic (not fixed at twenty-four hours); Kafka suits long retention and replay by offset. Model. Kinesis Data Streams: A W S-native streams and shards. Amazon M S K: Kafka topics and partitions. Pick when. Kinesis Data Streams: Simplest A W S integration, on-demand scaling. Amazon M S K: Existing Kafka apps, Kafka ecosystem, larger messages and long retention control. Capacity. Kinesis Data Streams: On-demand or shards. Amazon M S K: Brokers (Provisioned) or Serverless. Exam tip: "Migrate an on-premises Kafka application with no code changes" to Amazon M S K.

1.title: DynamoDB Streams
1.text: DynamoDB Streams. Records item-level changes (create, update, delete) in order, kept for twenty-four hours; each stream record appears exactly once, and order is kept per item. View types: keys only, new image, old image, new and old images; the type cannot be edited after the stream is set up. Typical use: a Lambda trigger that replicates, audits or enriches changes; a Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB integration is the choice for longer retention and more consumers. Enabling a stream has no performance impact on the table.

1.title: AWS DMS, Glue and Redshift as streaming sources
1.text: A W S D M S, Glue and Redshift as streaming sources. A W S D M S reads the transaction log of a source database and streams ongoing changes to targets such as Kinesis Data Streams, Kafka, S three and Redshift. A W S Glue streaming jobs read Kinesis or Kafka, process micro-batches with Spark Structured Streaming, and write to S three and other stores; they checkpoint progress. Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion reads from Kinesis or M S K into a materialized view that refreshes continuously.

2.title: Calling a Lambda Function from Kinesis
2.text: Calling a Lambda Function from Kinesis. You connect Lambda to a stream with an event source mapping: Lambda polls each shard and invokes your function with a batch of records from one shard. Standard consumer: shares the shard's two megabytes per second with other consumers. Enhanced fan-out consumer: a dedicated connection per shard, lower latency. Batch size and batching window: by default Lambda invokes as soon as records are available; a batching window of up to five minutes collects larger batches; the batch is also capped at six megabytes. Parallelization factor (one to ten): several concurrent batches per shard; order is still kept per partition key.

2.title: Calling a Lambda Function from Kinesis, continued
2.text: Calling a Lambda Function from Kinesis, continued. Errors: Lambda retries the failing batch and blocks that shard until it succeeds or the record expires; use bisect batch on function error, maximum retry attempts, maximum record age and an on-failure destination (S Q S, S N S (Simple Notification Service)) so one bad record does not stop the stream. Processing is at least once: make the function idempotent. Tumbling windows let a function aggregate records over a time window. To go faster: add shards, raise the parallelization factor, use enhanced fan-out, or reserve concurrency. Exam tip: "A poison record blocks a shard and the iterator age rises" to bisect on error, limit retries and record age, and send failures to an on-failure destination.

2.title: Fan-In and Fan-Out
2.text: Fan-In and Fan-Out. The figure shows this: Fan-in and fan-out: many producers write into one stream; standard consumers share two megabytes per second per shard, while each enhanced fan-out consumer gets its own two megabytes per second per shard.

2.title: Fan-In and Fan-Out, continued
2.text: Fan-In and Fan-Out, continued. Fan-in. Meaning: Many producers to one stream. How: Every producer calls PutRecord or uses the K P L (Kinesis Producer Library) (batching, aggregation); the partition key spreads the load; Firehose or M S K accept many senders. Fan-out (shared). Meaning: Several consumers read the same stream. How: Standard consumers share two megabytes per second per shard and five reads per second: more consumers means throttling and delay. Fan-out (enhanced). Meaning: Each consumer gets its own two megabytes per second per shard. How: Enhanced fan-out (RegisterStreamConsumer): up to twenty registered consumers per stream (fifty with on-demand advantage); H T T P or two push, lower latency, extra cost.

2.title: Fan-In and Fan-Out, continued
2.text: Fan-In and Fan-Out, continued. Fan-out by messaging. Meaning: One event to many subscribers. How: S N S topic with S Q S (Simple Queue Service) queues, or EventBridge rules. Kafka. Meaning: Many consumer groups read the same topic independently. How: Each consumer group keeps its own offset. Exam tip: "Five applications read the same stream and throttle each other" to enhanced fan-out.

2.title: Replayability
2.text: Replayability. Replayability is the ability to re-run ingestion over past data after a bug, a schema change or a new consumer. Where the history lives: Kinesis (retention twenty-four hours up to three hundred sixty-five days), M S K (per-topic retention and offsets), S three (a raw zone that keeps every record), DynamoDB Streams (twenty-four hours only). How to replay: start a consumer from the oldest record (trim horizon) or a timestamp (at timestamp), reset the Kafka offsets, rewind a Glue job bookmark, or redrive an S Q S dead-letter queue.

2.title: Replayability, continued
2.text: Replayability, continued. Design for it: keep raw data unchanged, make transformations idempotent (the same input gives the same output, no duplicates), use unique record I Ds or upserts, and write results to a new location or overwrite whole partitions. Firehose keeps no history: enable source record backup to S three if you need it. Exam tip: "Reprocess the last forty-eight hours after a bug fix" to a stream with at least forty-eight hours of retention (or raw data in S three) plus idempotent consumers.

2.title: Stateful and Stateless Data Transactions
2.text: Stateful and Stateless Data Transactions. Stateless: each record is processed on its own, with no memory of earlier records (filter, map, convert format, enrich with a lookup). Easy to scale and retry. Stateful: the result depends on earlier records: windows, running totals, joins, sessionization, de-duplication. The engine must keep state and checkpoint it. Services for stateful work: Managed Service for Apache Flink (state and checkpoints), Spark Structured Streaming in Glue or E M R (Elastic MapReduce), Lambda tumbling windows (small cases). Window types: tumbling (fixed, no overlap), sliding (overlapping), session (gap-based).

2.title: Stateful and Stateless Data Transactions, continued
2.text: Stateful and Stateless Data Transactions, continued. Stateful data transactions (a multi-step operation that must remember where it is) need a state store or checkpoint; stateless transactions carry everything in the request. Exam tip: "Count events per truck in five-minute windows" is stateful to Flink or Spark Structured Streaming. "Convert each record's timestamp format" is stateless to Lambda or Firehose transformation.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Kinesis Data Streams: Shards; partition key to shard to order per key. Data Firehose: Delivery, no replay; S three, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Iceberg, H T T P; buffer size or time; Lambda transform. M S K: Managed Kafka; topics, partitions, consumer groups; Provisioned or Serverless; M S K Connect; per-topic retention. DynamoDB Streams: Item changes, twenty-four hours, exactly once, ordered per item; four view types. D M S C D C (change data capture): Streams database changes to Kinesis, Kafka, S three. Lambda plus Kinesis: Event source mapping; batch from one shard; batching window up to five min; parallelization one to ten. Fan-out: Shared two megabytes per second per shard; enhanced fan-out equals own two megabytes per second per consumer (twenty consumers). Replay: Retention plus trim horizon or at timestamp; raw data in S three; idempotent consumers.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Kestrel Freight wants every truck reading delivered to Amazon S three as Parquet files partitioned by date, with no servers to manage and no custom consumer code. Which service should the data engineer use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Amazon Data Firehose delivers streaming data to S three without servers, can convert to Parquet and can partition by record fields. The others require you to build and run consumers.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Records for each truck must be processed in order, and traffic is spread evenly across thousands of trucks. How should the producer choose the partition key for Kinesis Data Streams? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Records with the same partition key go to the same shard and stay in order, and thousands of distinct truck I Ds spread the load. A constant key creates a hot shard; random values break per-truck order.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Four applications read the same Kinesis data stream and the consumers are slowed by throttling on the shared read throughput. What is the best way to fix this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Standard consumers share two megabytes per second per shard; enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own two megabytes per second per shard.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Select two. A Lambda function reads from a Kinesis data stream. One malformed record makes the function fail every time, and the stream's iterator age keeps growing. Which two settings help the stream keep moving? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Bisecting the batch isolates the bad record, and an on-failure destination with retry and age limits stops one record from blocking the shard. More shards do not remove a poison record, and disabling the mapping stops all processing.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A team must reprocess the last forty-eight hours of events after fixing a bug in a consumer. The events are in a Kinesis data stream with the default retention. What should the engineer do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The default retention is twenty-four hours, so older data is already gone for a forty-eight-hour replay; extend retention (up to three hundred sixty-five days) and read from the oldest record or a timestamp. Keeping raw data in S three is the longer-term answer.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. An existing on-premises Apache Kafka application must move to A W S with minimal code changes. Which service fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Amazon M S K runs open-source Apache Kafka, so existing clients and tools work without changes.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which workload is stateful? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A windowed count depends on earlier records and needs state and checkpoints. The other tasks treat each record independently.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: A. Question two: B. Question three: D. Question four: B and C. Question five: D. Question six: D. Question seven: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
